content: Public health surveillance involves the continuous, systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of data related to health events. This process is essential for guiding public health actions aimed at reducing morbidity and mortality and improving overall health outcomes. Surveillance systems fulfill at least eight critical public health functions. A key function of surveillance is the detection of outbreaks, which involves identifying an increase in disease frequency above the expected baseline. Outbreaks are often recognized through accumulated case reports of reportable diseases or by clinicians and laboratory personnel who notify public health officials about clusters of diseases. Due to the threat of terrorism and the increasing availability of electronic health data, existing surveillance systems are being enhanced, and new systems are being developed and implemented. These advancements aim to enable the early and comprehensive detection of outbreaks. The effectiveness of surveillance systems in early outbreak detection and response has not been fully established. Developing, enhancing, and managing these systems, as well as investigating false alarms, can incur significant costs. Evaluating the performance of public health surveillance systems for outbreak detection is necessary to determine the relative value of different approaches and to improve their efficiency in identifying outbreaks at the earliest stages. This report supplements existing CDC guidelines for evaluating public health surveillance systems. It provides a framework for assessing the timeliness of outbreak detection and balancing sensitivity, predictive value positive (PVP), and predictive value negative (PVN) in detecting outbreaks. The framework also encourages detailed descriptions of system design, operations, and experiences with outbreak detection. The framework is most effectively applied to systems with data that demonstrate the attributes of the system under evaluation. However, it can also be applied to systems in early development or planning stages by referencing published literature to support conclusions. Ideally, evaluations should compare the performance of the surveillance system under review to alternative systems and provide an assessment of their relative usefulness for early outbreak detection. Early detection of outbreaks can be achieved through three primary methods: 1) timely and complete receipt, review, and investigation of disease case reports, including prompt recognition and reporting by healthcare providers and laboratories in compliance with disease reporting laws; 2) improving the ability to recognize patterns indicative of potential outbreaks early in their course, such as through analytic tools that enhance the predictive value of data or by lowering the threshold for investigating possible outbreaks; and 3) utilizing new types of data that can signal an outbreak earlier in its course. New data types, such as healthcare product purchases, work or school absences, presenting symptoms to healthcare providers, or laboratory test orders, have been used to enhance surveillance. These data types reflect events that may precede a clinical diagnosis. The foundation of communicable disease surveillance in the United States is the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System (NNDSS). This system includes a list of diseases and laboratory findings of public health interest, case definitions for surveillance, and a process for transmitting case reports from local to state to federal levels. Effective surveillance requires two-way communication between public health agencies and the clinical community. Clinicians and laboratories report cases and clusters of reportable and unusual diseases, while health departments provide consultation on case diagnosis and management, alerts, surveillance summaries, and public health recommendations and policies. Faster, more specific, and affordable diagnostic methods and decision-support tools for diseases with significant outbreak potential could improve the timely recognition of reportable diseases. Ongoing outreach, education, and 24-hour access to public health professionals are necessary to enhance the reporting of urgent health threats. Electronic laboratory reporting (ELR), which involves the automated transfer of designated data from laboratory databases to public health repositories, improves the timeliness and completeness of reporting notifiable conditions. ELR can also serve as a model for electronic reporting of a broader range of clinical information. Comprehensive surveillance efforts support timely investigation and tracking of cases once an outbreak is recognized. They also address data needs for managing public health responses to outbreaks or terrorist events. Statistical tools for pattern recognition and aberration detection can screen data for patterns warranting further public health investigation. These tools enhance the recognition of subtle or obscure outbreak patterns. Automated analysis and visualization tools reduce the need for frequent and intensive manual analysis of surveillance data. Syndromic surveillance systems use data that are not diagnostic of a disease but may indicate the early stages of an outbreak. These systems monitor disease indicators in real-time or near real-time to detect outbreaks earlier and more comprehensively than traditional public health methods. The distinguishing feature of syndromic surveillance is the use of indicator data types. For example, laboratory test requests can serve as an outbreak indicator by tracking excess volumes of test requests for diseases that typically cause outbreaks. Syndromic surveillance for terrorism preparedness focuses on outbreak detection. Enhanced case finding and monitoring the course and population characteristics of recognized outbreaks are additional potential benefits. Syndromic surveillance has been used effectively in resource-poor settings for sexually transmitted disease detection and control when laboratory confirmation is not feasible. However, it is not intended for early detection of single cases or limited outbreaks because the early clinical manifestations of diseases potentially caused by terrorism are common and nonspecific. The framework for evaluating public health surveillance systems is organized into four categories: system description, outbreak detection, experience, and conclusions and recommendations. A comprehensive evaluation addresses all four categories. The purpose of the surveillance system should be explicitly described, including its intended uses, the context in which it operates, and the types of outbreaks it is designed to detect. Stakeholders, including data providers and users, should be identified to define who the system serves and provide context for evaluation results. All aspects of the system's operation should be described in detail to validate the system's description and understand the complexity and resources required for its operation. Detailed system descriptions facilitate evaluation by highlighting variations in system operation relevant to performance. The ability of a system to reliably detect outbreaks at the earliest possible stage depends on the timely capture and processing of data, the validity of the data for measuring conditions of interest, and the detection methods applied to processed surveillance data. The validity of a system for outbreak detection requires an operational definition of an outbreak. Confirmation of an outbreak depends on past experience, the severity and communicability of the condition, confidence in the diagnosis, public health concern, available prevention or control options, and the resources required and available to respond. Different approaches to outbreak detection should be evaluated under the same conditions to isolate the unique features of the system. Data for evaluating and comparing surveillance systems can be obtained from naturally occurring outbreaks or through simulation. Standardized classification of system and outbreak factors enables comparison of experiences across systems. Routine reporting of outbreak detection successes and failures should be automated where possible.
